newsitem.title: ISRAEL: U.S. official visits family of dead Arab boy.
newsitem.headline: U.S. official visits family of dead Arab boy.

text.p: A representative of the U.S. government paid a condolence call in the West Bank on Wednesday to the family of a Palestinian boy who Arab witnesses said was killed by a Jewish settler.

U.S Consul-General in Jerusalem, Edward Abington, said his visit to the family of 11-year-old Hilmi Shousha in the village of Husan, near Bethlehem, was intended to demonstrate U.S. support for Palestinian-Israeli peacemaking.
"I convey my condolences and the condolences of the United States government," Abington told the Shousha family. "It's always a greater tragedy when a child dies as a result of violence."

Asked about the objective of his trip, Abington said: "I think that it's to show that the United States is committed to the peace process and that the United States wants the peace process to succeed so that no children, Palestinian children or Israeli children...will be hurt or killed."

Hilmi died in an Israeli hospital on Monday, one day after the security chief of a neighbouring Jewish settlement struck him on the head with his pistol and stomped on him while the boy was returning from school, a classmate said.

Other settlers say Nahum Kurman chased Hilmi after he and other boys threw stones at Israeli vehicles but did not beat him. An autopsy showed Shousha died from a brain haemorrhage caused by a sharp blow to the neck.

Kurman has been in police custody since Sunday. A magistrates court on Tuesday remanded him until Friday while police prepared charges. Police took witnesses to the site on Wednesday to re-enact the incident.

The killing came against the backdrop of rising tension between Jewish settlers and Palestinians over Israeli-PLO negotiations on a long overdue Israeli army redeployment in the West Bank town of Hebron.
Settlers oppose the U.S.-sponsored Israeli-PLO peace moves.

Grief and anger at the killing turned violent during Hilmi's funeral on Tuesday when Palestinian mourners attacked Israeli traffic on a road used by settlers. Israeli soldiers opened fire at the demonstrators and four people were overcome by teargas.
Clearly moved by the boy's death, Abington told the Shousha family that he shared their grief and assured them that the Israeli government was investigating the incident.

"I have a six-year-old and she is the most precious thing that I have and if anything happened to her it would be devastating to me, so I know the Shousha family must be heartbroken at the death of their son," he said.

"I know the government of Israel is investigating this incident. I know that they have under detention a suspect and I am confident that the government of Israel will be fair and evenhanded in their investigations," Abington said.
